description: We are Team Numero Uno, a group of third-year Computer Science and Engineering students at UPES, Dehradun. We share a passion for computer science and a fascination with space, and the Earth Systems Trend Detective challenge brought both together. We joined forces to build Tellus, a tool that turns NASA's Earth data into answers anyone can understand and trust. Our aim was simple: help people tell a real change in our planet from ordinary variation, and show the evidence behind every answer.
summary: Tellus is a web app that turns NASA Earth data into answers anyone can trust. You ask a question as a sentence, for example "Is the Arctic getting warmer over the last 45 years?", and Tellus answers as a sentence: "The Arctic is getting warmer, and it has been clear since 2002", with the rate (+0.46 °C per decade), its uncertainty, and the year the change became statistically clear. It covers the whole planet with NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data from 1981 to 2025, plus NASA satellite and model records from Giovanni, KNMI and NOAA. What makes Tellus different is honesty you can see. Its tests allow for years that cluster, a one-click shuffle shows what "significant" really means, two places can be compared with a formal test, and Tellus checks its own numbers against published science. An AI assistant answers questions in plain words, using only numbers the engine computed.
details:
Team Numero Uno. Live app: https://tellus-web.onrender.com · Source code: https://github.com/Mrigank005/Tellus

What it does

Tellus answers the challenge's five questions (which variable, what is changing, where, how much and whether it is significant) for any of 22 regions, any place you draw on the map, and the whole Earth.

  • A guided journey for newcomers.
    • Hero: a tree-ring disc shows 45 years of global temperature, one ring per year.
    • Ask: a sentence builder ("Is [place] getting [warmer/wetter/...] over [years] [season]?") replaces forms, above a world map of the real trend.
    • Answer: the verdict reads as a sentence and a specimen label (rate per decade, 95% interval, year it became clear, possible shift year). A four-part story panel lights up the matching part of the chart.
    • Is it real, or just weather? The record is read three ways: the naive test, 500 live random shuffles of the real years, and Tellus's persistence-corrected test. For the Arctic, none of the 500 shuffled records matches the real trend.
  • A field desk for deeper work.
    • Global map: per-cell trends over 207,936 grid cells, with false discovery rate control across the map.
    • Regions: draw any region and Tellus fetches its record live from NASA POWER.
    • Comparisons: compare two places with a difference-of-trends test. The Arctic warms +0.27 °C per decade faster than the tropics, 95% interval +0.16 to +0.37, p < 0.001.
    • Sensitivity: a start × end year window scan and a season × window grid.
    • Cross-checks: model against satellite and observation (MERRA-2 against GPCP rainfall, and against IMERG, AIRS, OMI and GLDAS series).
    • Also: an opposite-trends finder, area shares of change, exploratory events, and CSV, provenance and report export.
  • Ask Tellus, an AI assistant. It understands questions in plain words, compares places when two are named, answers only from engine results with the evidence listed, checks every number before showing it, and falls back to a rules-based guide if the AI is unavailable.
  • A field guide to 21 measurements, four detective case files with guided tours, a "Check our work" ledger, Day and Dusk themes that follow the device, and a phone layout.

How it works

  • Pipeline: a Python pipeline fetches and aggregates NASA data, then computes Sen's slope with a 95% interval and the Mann-Kendall test.
  • Statistics:
    • Persistence: significance is adjusted for year-to-year persistence (AR(1) effective sample size), and the naive result is shown alongside.
    • Multiple places: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate control across maps.
    • Further tests: time of emergence, Pettitt change point, detection horizon, window robustness and a difference-of-trends test.
  • Where it runs: the same statistics are implemented in TypeScript and run in the browser.
  • Verification: they are parity-tested against the Python reference on 300 series and hundreds of special cases. 193 Python tests and 28 TypeScript tests cover calibration, robustness, area weighting and the assistant's grounding.

Why it matters

  • Climate claims are everywhere, and a chart alone cannot tell a real change from a run of unusual years.
  • Tellus gives students, teachers, journalists and curious citizens a defensible answer, and shows them why it is defensible. For example, Sahel monsoon rainfall rises +35 mm per decade and looks significant under the naive test (p = 0.019), but wet years cluster: about 15 independent years of 45, corrected p = 0.18. Tellus shows both and explains the difference.
  • Checked against independent science: 3 pass, 4 partial, 1 miss and 1 not comparable, all published in full in the app.

Tools

  • Code: Python (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, FastAPI), React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts.
  • Hosting: Render.
  • AI assistant model: NVIDIA Nemotron via OpenRouter.

What's next

  • Per-cell global maps for the satellite records.
  • MODIS, GRACE, CERES and sea-ice layers.
  • A "scan this place" ranking of every measurement.
  • A time-lapse 3D globe and seasonal Mann-Kendall.
  • An MCP interface so other AI tools can query Tellus's verified engine.
  • A classroom mode with shareable investigations.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 monthly regional and global grid, 8 variables, 1981–2025)
MERRA-2 reanalysis (model behind the NASA POWER grid, GMAO)
NASA GES DISC Giovanni (area-averaged regional series)
GPM IMERG Final Monthly V07 (satellite rainfall)
GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model v2.1 (runoff, evapotranspiration, soil moisture)
AIRS/Aqua L3 monthly v7 (surface air temperature)
NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 (validates the global warming rate)
projectRefs: KNMI Climate Explorer (challenge resource): NOAA OISST sea-surface temperature, NOAA CDR NDVI, CMORPH rainfall
NOAA NCEI Climate Data Online (challenge resource): De Bilt station temperature, 1901–2025
HadCRUT5 (Met Office Hadley Centre / UEA CRU, validation)
React, TypeScript, Vite, zustand (MIT); NumPy, SciPy, xarray, netCDF4 (open source)
Gloock and Atkinson Hyperlegible fonts (SIL Open Font License)
OpenRouter API serving NVIDIA Nemotron (Ask Tellus language model)
